requirements: Reproduce FluxMoE, a MoE inference system that decouples expert parameters from persistent GPU residency via expert paging, and validate its throughput gains over vLLM baselines.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware, software, and framework environment matching the paper's evaluation testbed has been prepared.
Hardware platform matches the paper's single-node testbed configuration.
The evaluation server node uses Intel Xeon Platinum 8358 processors with a total of 128 vCPUs available to the runtime.
The server is provisioned with 2 TiB of host DRAM to support pinned host memory for the CPU offload backend.
The node has at least 3 TB of local disk storage for holding model weights, compressed artifacts, and dataset caches.
The node contains four NVIDIA L40 PCIe GPUs, each with 48 GB of GDDR6 memory with ECC support, all visible to the runtime.
The GPUs are attached over PCIe such that host-to-device DMA bandwidth used by the CPU offload backend matches the tens-of-GB/s regime assumed by the paper.
GPU software stack (CUDA driver/runtime and VMM support) required by PagedTensor is installed and functional.
A CUDA toolkit version providing the Virtual Memory Management APIs (cuMemMap, cuMemUnmap, cuMemAddressReserve, cuMemCreate) is installed and linkable from the FluxMoE C++ extension.
The NVIDIA driver on the testbed supports CUDA VMM APIs on L40 GPUs and exposes granularity/allocation flags used by PagedTensor's ring-buffer physical block pool.

A smoke test allocates a virtual address range, binds/unbinds physical GPU blocks via cuMemMap/cuMemUnmap, and verifies that data written through the mapping is readable, confirming VMM functionality on the testbed.
Python and deep learning framework environment matching FluxMoE's implementation base is set up.
vLLM version 0.10.2 is installed as the underlying serving framework, and FluxMoE's ~20 LoC Python interface patch integrates cleanly with this exact version.
PyTorch and Triton versions compatible with vLLM v0.10.2 and with CUDA VMM usage are installed so unmodified inference kernels reference PagedTensor virtual addresses without errors.

The FluxMoE C++ extension (~3.1K LoC) and Python module (~2.1K LoC) build against the installed CUDA/PyTorch versions and expose the PagedTensor, storage backend, and residency planner APIs to the vLLM worker process.
Serving/parallelism deployment configuration matches the paper's evaluation setup for the two evaluated MoE models.
Tensor parallelism can be configured at degree TP=4 on the four L40 GPUs for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct experiments, and the model launches successfully under FluxMoE.
Tensor parallelism can be configured at degree TP=2 on a subset of two L40 GPUs for the capacity-bound Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct experiments, matching the paper's Exp#2/Exp#3 configuration.
The serving launcher exposes configurable batch sizes in {32, 64, 128, 256} and context lengths in {1024, 2048, 3072, 4096} tokens as evaluation sweep parameters.
The deployment focuses on the decode-phase / sustained-generation workload and reports aggregate throughput (tokens/s) as the primary metric, rather than TTFT or single-user TPOT.
Baseline serving configurations (vLLM, vLLM-O, FluxMoE-H) needed for comparison experiments are installed and runnable on the same testbed.
A stock vLLM v0.10.2 baseline can be launched on the testbed with the same TP settings as FluxMoE for the performance-bound regime experiments.

A vLLM-O variant is available that uses PagedTensor with expanded buffer blocks, keeps experts of the front 87.5% of layers uncompressed in GPU memory, and offloads the final 12.5% of layer experts to host DRAM with prefetching overlapped across layers.

A FluxMoE-H hybrid ablation baseline is available in which the front 87.5% of expert layers are fully compressed and GPU-resident and the final 12.5% of layers are fully offloaded to host DRAM at whole-layer granularity (no bandwidth-balanced hierarchy).
The two MoE models (Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct) and the ShareGPT dataset used for evaluation are available and usable.
Both MoE models used in the paper have been acquired with correct architecture and precision.
Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct model checkpoint has been downloaded/acquired from the official Hugging Face repository (mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1) and is loadable.
Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct model checkpoint has been downloaded/acquired from the official Hugging Face repository and is loadable.
Code has been implemented to load both MoE models in BFloat16 precision (matching the paper's assumed data-type width used for the compression and memory-footprint analysis).
Model structural parameters match the specifications reported in Table 1 and Section 6.1 of the paper.
Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct loaded configuration reports 32 MoE layers and a total parameter count of approximately 47B, matching the paper's Table 1.
Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct loaded configuration reports 48 MoE layers and a total parameter count of approximately 80B, matching the paper's Section 6.1 description.
The measured on-disk/loaded memory footprint of Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct in BFloat16 is approximately 94 GB, matching Table 1.
The measured on-disk/loaded memory footprint of Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct in BFloat16 is approximately 160 GB, matching Table 1.
The ShareGPT dataset used for evaluation workloads has been acquired and processed into the workload configurations described in Section 6.1.
The ShareGPT dataset (as referenced from the Hugging Face collection linked in the paper's reference [4]) has been downloaded and stored locally.

Code has been implemented to sample requests from the ShareGPT dataset to construct evaluation workloads spanning batch sizes {32, 64, 128, 256} and context lengths {1024, 2048, 3072, 4096} tokens, matching Section 6.1.

Code has been implemented to tokenize/truncate/pad sampled ShareGPT prompts to the requested context lengths using each model's tokenizer, producing well-formed request batches for the serving system.
The memory footprint characterization of MoE models and the KV-cache-vs-throughput relationship described in Section 2 have been reproduced.
Profiling infrastructure to characterize GPU memory composition and throughput vs. KV cache capacity on MoE models has been implemented.
Code has been implemented to deploy MoE models via vLLM with tensor parallelism degree 4 (single node, four GPUs) as the characterization testbed described in Section 2.

Code has been implemented to sweep the batch size across {32, 64, 128, 256} at a fixed context length of 4,096 tokens, and to sweep the context length across {1024, 2048, 3072, 4096} at a fixed batch size of 256, driving the profiling runs.
Code has been implemented to break down per-GPU memory consumption during inference into the four categories reported in Figure 1: model weights, KV cache, linear attention state, and others.
Code has been implemented to configure vLLM's KV cache budget to specific target sizes (20 GiB, 40 GiB, 60 GiB) via GPU memory utilization settings for the throughput-vs-KV-capacity study.
Code has been implemented to measure sustained decode throughput in tokens/second, aggregating across the workload, to feed the KV-capacity-vs-throughput characterization.
The parameter-scale comparison between dense and MoE models reported in Table 1 has been reproduced.

Code has been implemented that loads the four models (Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct) and reports their parameter counts and on-disk/GPU memory footprints in GB.
The measured memory footprint of Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct matches the 94 GB value (with 47B parameters) reported in Table 1.
The measured memory footprint of Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct matches the 160 GB value (with 80B parameters) reported in Table 1.
The MoE-to-dense size ratios computed from the measurements match the claims that Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct is 6.7x larger than Mistral-7B and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct is 5.4x larger than Qwen2.5-14B.
The Figure 1 memory-composition characterization of Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct has been reproduced.
Code has been implemented that produces the Figure 1(a) memory-composition breakdown for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct at context length 4,096 across batch sizes {32, 64, 128, 256}.
Code has been implemented that produces the Figure 1(b) memory-composition breakdown for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct at batch size 256 across context lengths {1024, 2048, 3072, 4096}.

The measured breakdown confirms that model weights occupy a substantially larger share of GPU memory than the KV cache for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct across the profiled configurations, matching the qualitative claim in Section 2.1.
The Figure 2 relationship between KV cache capacity and inference throughput on Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct has been reproduced.

Code has been implemented that measures Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct decode throughput on the characterization testbed under KV cache budgets of 20 GiB, 40 GiB, and 60 GiB while sweeping batch size from 32 to 256 at context length 4,096 (Figure 2(a)).

Code has been implemented that measures Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct decode throughput under KV cache budgets of 20 GiB, 40 GiB, and 60 GiB while sweeping context length from 1,024 to 4,096 tokens at batch size 256 (Figure 2(b)).
At batch size 128 and context length 4,096, expanding the KV cache budget from 20 GiB to 60 GiB increases measured throughput by approximately 58.8%, matching the claim in Section 2.2.
Under a fixed 20 GiB KV budget at batch size 256, extending the context length from 1,024 to 4,096 tokens produces approximately a 66.7% throughput drop, matching the claim in Section 2.2.

The 60 GiB KV configuration reduces the context-length-induced throughput loss (from 1,024 to 4,096 tokens at batch size 256) by approximately 53.5% relative to the 20 GiB configuration, matching the claim in Section 2.2.

The measurements confirm that within a fixed KV budget, throughput increases with batch size until the KV cache saturates and CPU-GPU swapping begins, reproducing the qualitative curve shape of Figure 2(a).

The PagedTensor tensor-virtualization mechanism (three-tier abstraction, stable virtual addresses, CUDA VMM-based physical block mapping, and cross-stream synchronization protocol) has been implemented per Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1.
The three-tier tensor abstraction (tensor handle, tensor buffer, tensor storage) that decouples logical expert-tensor identity from physical GPU residency is implemented per Section 3.2.

Code has been implemented that treats each expert as two independently paged weight tensors (a fused gate/up-projection tensor and a down-projection tensor), each managed with its own tensor handle, so the two per-expert weight tensors can be transferred in parallel and can be sized with different physical allocations.

Code has been implemented that creates an 8-byte tensor handle per expert weight tensor, exposing invariant metadata (shape, dtype, device placement) and a fixed reserved range in the GPU virtual address space, so unmodified inference kernels reference the handle as if it were a persistently resident tensor.

Code has been implemented that maintains a pre-allocated pool of reusable physical tensor buffers, each sized precisely to its target weight tensor, and recycles all buffers of a layer once the layer completes execution.

Code has been implemented that provisions exactly 4L tensor buffers per rank (2L for the currently executing layer and 2L for the layer being prefetched, with two buffers per expert and L experts per layer), realizing the two-layer sliding residency window baseline.

Code has been implemented that maintains a tensor-storage tier serving as the persistent backing store for all N x L expert weight tensors, spanning compressed GPU memory and host DRAM and supplying data into tensor buffers during materialization.

Code has been implemented that models each tensor page as transitioning through the four-state lifecycle Unmapped -> Loading -> Resident -> Evicting, with explicit state tracking used to gate mapping, load, use, and unmap operations.
The stable virtualized tensor address space and physical block pool of PagedTensor are implemented per the formal model in Section 4.1.

Code has been implemented that maintains two independent virtual address spaces V^(d) (one for the fused gate/up-projection tensor type d=1 and one for the down-projection tensor type d=2), each reserving a contiguous GPU virtual address region of size N * L * sigma^(d).

Code has been implemented that assigns each tensor page P_{i,j}^(d) a deterministic virtual address equal to v_0^(d) + (i-1) * L * sigma^(d) + (j-1) * sigma^(d), and this address is invariant across the entire inference session regardless of physical block binding.
The virtual address exposed for a given (layer i, expert j, tensor type d) remains bit-identical across many map/unmap cycles and across many decode iterations, verifying pointer stability.
Code has been implemented that maintains, per tensor type d, a physical block pool F^(d) of exactly 2L physical blocks each of size sigma^(d), for a total of 4L physical blocks across both types.

The mapping function enforces the deterministic-mapping invariant that at any instant each tensor page is bound to at most one physical block (|map(P_{i,j}^(d))| <= 1) and each physical block is bound to at most one page.

The physical block pool with 4L blocks correctly backs a much larger logical tensor space of 2NL pages (block reuse invariant), demonstrated by successfully serving models where N*L >> 2L (e.g., 32-48 layers with 8-512 experts per layer) without additional physical allocations.
The CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM)-based physical-block mapping backend that binds/unbinds physical GPU memory to the reserved virtual ranges is implemented per Section 5.

Code has been implemented that reserves the contiguous per-type GPU virtual address ranges using CUDA VMM APIs (cuMemAddressReserve or equivalent) at initialization, sized to hold all N*L pages per tensor type.
Code has been implemented that allocates the 4L physical memory blocks as CUDA VMM physical allocations (cuMemCreate) and manages them as a ring buffer for dynamic remapping.
Code has been implemented that maps a physical block to a tensor page's virtual address via cuMemMap (plus cuMemSetAccess) during the Map step of layer materialization (Algorithm 1 line 8).
Code has been implemented that unmaps a physical block from a tensor page via cuMemUnmap when the block is recycled for a new layer (Algorithm 1 line 6), returning it to the free pool.
Code has been implemented that exposes each mapped tensor page to PyTorch/Triton kernels as an ordinary contiguous tensor at its stable virtual address without any modification to compute kernels.
The virtual-to-physical mapping is resolved entirely outside the compute kernel (ahead of kernel launch), with no in-kernel address-arithmetic or indirection introduced into MoE compute kernels.
After a page has been mapped, an AsyncLoad (DMA copy from CPU pinned memory or decompression kernel output) correctly populates the bound physical block with the expert's parameter data.

The forward proxy and layer-wise materialization orchestration described in Section 3.1 and Algorithm 1 (MaterializeLayer / ForwardPass) are implemented so that expert paging is transparent to the underlying model forward pass.
Code has been implemented for a forward proxy that intercepts the model forward pass and, before layer i begins execution, ensures all experts in E_i are physically resident in GPU memory.

Code has been implemented that concurrently releases the physical blocks of layer i-1's experts and asynchronously prefetches layer i+1's experts from tensor storage while layer i is executing, realizing the sliding residency window R_i = E_i union E_{i+1}.

Code has been implemented for the MaterializeLayer(i, N, iter) procedure that, for each tensor type d in {1,2}, performs (a) the WAR wait on the target layer's compute event, (b) block recycling for that target layer, (c) Map for T_i^(d), (d) AsyncLoad on stream_load^(d), and (e) RecordEvent event_i^{load(d)}.

The target layer for block reclamation is computed as ((i - 3 + N) mod N) + 1 (i.e., the second preceding layer with cyclic wrap-around across iteration boundaries) exactly as specified in Algorithm 1 line 4.
Code has been implemented for the cold-start bypass in Algorithm 1 line 3: when iter == 1 and i <= 2 the WAR wait and block recycling are skipped because the physical block pool is empty.

Code has been implemented for the ForwardPass(i) procedure that, for each d, waits on event_i^{load(d)} on stream_comp (RAW barrier), launches the MoE kernels for layer i on stream_comp, and records event_i^{comp} on stream_comp.
The cross-stream synchronization protocol enforcing WAR and RAW ordering via CUDA streams and events is implemented per Algorithm 1 and Section 4.1.

Code has been implemented that provisions per MoE layer, per rank, two dedicated CUDA loading streams (stream_load^(1) for gate/up-projection and stream_load^(2) for down-projection) so that the two weight tensors of a layer are transferred concurrently.
Code has been implemented that maintains a single dedicated inference-compute stream stream_comp separate from the loading streams, on which the MoE forward kernels are launched.

The WAR ordering constraint is enforced: a stream_load^(d) waits (via cudaStreamWaitEvent on event_target^{comp}) for the target layer's forward-pass completion before unmapping/recycling any of that layer's physical blocks (Algorithm 1 line 5).

The RAW ordering constraint is enforced: stream_comp waits on both event_i^{load(1)} and event_i^{load(2)} before launching any compute kernel for layer i (Algorithm 1 line 15), preventing kernels from reading uninitialized or partially populated blocks.

Code has been implemented that records event_i^{load(d)} on stream_load^(d) immediately after the AsyncLoad/decompression for layer i, tensor type d, completes (Algorithm 1 line 10), and records event_i^{comp} on stream_comp immediately after the layer-i compute kernels are enqueued (Algorithm 1 line 18).

Cross-stream synchronization is achieved using CUDA event barriers (cudaEventRecord + cudaStreamWaitEvent) exclusively, without inserting any blocking host-side synchronization primitives (cudaDeviceSynchronize / cudaStreamSynchronize) on the inference critical path.

Under stress tests with adversarial timing (delayed loads or fast compute), the synchronization protocol prevents any compute kernel from launching against a page whose state is not Resident, and prevents any physical block from being unmapped while an in-flight kernel still references it.
The four PagedTensor design invariants (stable virtual addresses, deterministic mapping, safe remapping, block reuse) are enforced end-to-end and are observable in behavioral tests.

A behavioral test demonstrates that a compute kernel referencing a tensor handle observes correct expert parameter values across many remap cycles (e.g., over a full multi-iteration decode), producing bitwise identical outputs to a weight-resident reference run.

A test asserts that no tensor page is ever simultaneously mapped to two physical blocks and no physical block is ever simultaneously mapped to two pages during a full inference run (deterministic mapping invariant).
The Python/vLLM integration modifies only about 20 lines of vLLM Python code to interface the framework with PagedTensor, matching the non-intrusive integration described in Section 5.
PagedTensor's runtime cost and memory-footprint claims match the measured numbers reported in the paper.

In a configuration where all experts are uncompressed and GPU-resident (buffers extended to hold the full uncompressed expert set, no decompression, no CPU offloading), the PagedTensor management overhead versus native vLLM stays negligible across the swept batch sizes and context lengths, i.e., FluxMoE throughput closely aligns with vLLM in Exp#4 (Figure 10).

The peak PagedTensor management overhead on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct with all experts uncompressed and GPU-resident occurs at batch size 64 and context length 4096 tokens, and equals approximately 3.0% throughput reduction relative to native vLLM.

The mandatory GPU-resident expert footprint imposed by PagedTensor's two-layer sliding window equals 2/N of the full model's expert capacity (i.e., for a model with N MoE layers, only the physical blocks for two layers of experts are simultaneously resident).

The bandwidth-balanced expert storage hierarchy with compressed GPU backend (selective Huffman coding of exponents) and CPU offload backend (pinned DRAM + async DMA) has been implemented per Section 4.2.
The storage hierarchy model implements bandwidth-proportional allocation across K heterogeneous backends.

Code has been implemented that defines a storage hierarchy abstraction consisting of a set of backends S = {S_1, ..., S_K}, each exposing an effective loading bandwidth B_k, and each capable of holding a fraction of expert parameters.
Code has been implemented that computes, for each backend S_k, the fraction x_k = B_k / sum(B_j) so that expert parameters are placed across backends in proportion to their effective bandwidth.

Code has been implemented that estimates per-layer expert loading latency tau_load_layer(i) as max_k( (x_k * P_layer) / B_k ) and aggregates tau_load across all N layers for use by the residency planner.

Given equal expected loading times across backends under the bandwidth-proportional allocation, the implementation's placement routine assigns fractions x_k that make all backends complete their per-layer transfers within a small tolerance (all backend-finish-times are within a few percent of each other) in a two-backend GPU+CPU configuration.
The compressed GPU backend stores expert parameters using selective Huffman coding of exponents and reconstructs them on demand with a GPU decompression kernel.

Compression is applied only to expert parameters (fused gate/up-projection and down-projection weights); all non-expert weights (e.g., attention projections, embeddings, router weights) remain uncompressed and GPU-resident.
Code has been implemented that splits each BFloat16 expert weight into its sign bit, exponent bits (8 bits), and mantissa bits (7 bits), operating separately on these bit fields.

The offline compression pipeline builds a Huffman code table from the empirical exponent distribution of expert weights and encodes only the exponent bit field, leaving sign and mantissa bits stored in their raw uncompressed form.

Compression is performed offline before inference begins, and the compressed exponents together with raw sign/mantissa bits are loaded into GPU memory at model initialization rather than being compressed on the inference critical path.

A high-throughput CUDA/GPU decompression kernel has been implemented that consumes Huffman-encoded exponents together with raw sign/mantissa bits and materializes original BFloat16 expert weight tensors into the target physical block buffers.

The decompression kernel is invoked on a dedicated CUDA loading stream so that decompression of layer i+1's experts overlaps with layer i's forward pass, without introducing implicit synchronization on the compute stream.

Applying the selective Huffman compression to BFloat16 experts of Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct reduces the on-device expert storage size by approximately 20% relative to the uncompressed BFloat16 baseline.

The exponent distribution of expert weights in the target MoE models is highly concentrated (sharp probability peak, low entropy) while the mantissa distribution is close to uniform, matching the compressibility pattern reported in Figure 5.

Decoded expert weight tensors are bitwise-identical to the original uncompressed BFloat16 tensors (lossless round-trip), verified by comparing decompressed outputs against source parameters for all expert weight tensors.

The measured effective decompression bandwidth of the compressed GPU backend on the L40 testbed reaches hundreds of GB/s per GPU, sufficient to keep the decompression cost hidden within the preceding layer's forward pass window.
The CPU offload backend stores expert weights in pinned host DRAM and streams them to GPU via asynchronous DMA over PCIe.
Code has been implemented that allocates expert weight tensors assigned to the CPU backend in pinned (page-locked) host DRAM to enable high-bandwidth asynchronous DMA transfers.

Host-to-device transfers of CPU-resident expert weights are issued as asynchronous cudaMemcpyAsync (or equivalent) operations on the dedicated loading CUDA stream, and never as synchronous blocking copies.
The CPU backend prefetches expert parameters for layer i+1 concurrently with layer i's forward pass, sized such that in-flight data is bounded by the two-layer sliding residency window.

The measured PCIe host-to-device transfer bandwidth achieved by the CPU offload backend during expert prefetching reaches tens of GB/s on the L40 PCIe testbed, close to the platform's effective PCIe bandwidth ceiling.
Dual-stream pipelining and integration with PagedTensor enable full compute-I/O overlap across the storage hierarchy.

A custom CUDA stream pool has been implemented that assigns two dedicated loading streams per MoE layer, one for the fused gate/up-projection tensors and one for the down-projection tensors, so that these two weight tensors are transferred/decompressed concurrently.

The compressed GPU backend and CPU offload backend operate on independent loading streams simultaneously so that decompression from GPU-resident compressed storage and PCIe DMA from host DRAM run in parallel within the same layer's loading window.

The storage hierarchy writes decompressed / DMA'd expert weights directly into the physical block buffers managed by PagedTensor and hands off ownership via the same CUDA-event synchronization protocol used by PagedTensor's materialization phase.

For each expert, the routing between the compressed GPU backend and the CPU offload backend is selected at initialization/planning time based on the bandwidth-proportional fractions, and the placement is recorded in a per-expert metadata table used by the loader.

In the capacity-bound configuration matching Exp#2 (Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, TP=2, ~12.5% CPU offload), the bandwidth-balanced hierarchy yields measurable throughput gains over FluxMoE-H (which uses strict whole-layer partitioning without bandwidth balancing), reproducing the ~22-29% improvement at batch size 256 across 1,024-4,096 token contexts.
Configuration and instrumentation for the storage hierarchy are exposed so the residency planner and end-to-end evaluation can drive it.

The storage hierarchy exposes a configuration interface to specify the compressed-GPU vs. CPU-offloaded fractions (equivalently the residency level alpha) at initialization and to change them at runtime under planner control.

The storage hierarchy reports per-backend effective bandwidth and per-layer loading latency measurements that the budget-aware residency planner consumes to estimate tau_load and the compute-to-load ratio rho.

A configuration mode is provided that disables the CPU offload backend and stores all experts (compressed) in the GPU backend, matching the setup used in Exp#1 (performance-bound regime for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct).

The closed-loop residency planner that dynamically adjusts the expert residency level based on the compute-to-load ratio under a GPU memory budget has been implemented per Section 4.3 and Algorithm 2.
Latency profiling and estimation primitives required by the planner have been implemented.

Code has been implemented to offline-profile the idealized per-iteration forwarding latency tau_comp(theory) in a weight-resident configuration (all uncompressed parameters and the KV cache permanently GPU-resident) as the theoretical minimum execution time.

Code has been implemented to re-profile tau_comp(theory) whenever the serving configuration changes substantially (e.g., batch size or context length shifts) so that the reference latency stays representative of the current workload.
Code has been implemented to compute the per-layer loading latency tau_load_layer(i) as the maximum over the K storage backends of (x_k * P_layer / B_k), reflecting concurrent backend operation.
Code has been implemented to compute the aggregate per-iteration loading demand tau_load as the sum of tau_load_layer(i) over all N MoE layers.

The estimator of tau_load updates when residency level alpha changes, using the storage-hierarchy bandwidth model from Section 4.2 to reflect the new expert placement across the compressed GPU and CPU offload backends.
The compute-to-load ratio rho and its use as the planner's control signal have been implemented.
Code has been implemented to compute the compute-to-load ratio rho = tau_comp(theory) / tau_load per iteration as the planner's control signal.
The planner targets the operating point rho approximately equal to 1, where expert materialization and forwarding are perfectly overlapped, as the ideal steady state.
The planner focuses residency adaptation on the autoregressive decoding phase and skips adjustment during compute-dominated prefill (where rho >> 1 naturally hides loading behind computation).
The residency control model that adjusts alpha via a rho-driven asymmetric threshold policy has been implemented.

The planner exposes an expert residency level alpha in (0, 1] representing the fraction of expert parameters resident in GPU memory (dense or compressed), with the remaining (1 - alpha) streamed from the CPU backend.
When rho > 1 (compute-bound), the planner decreases alpha to free GPU memory for the KV cache, following Algorithm 2 line 5.
When rho < theta (default theta = 0.9), the planner increases alpha to promote more experts into GPU residency and reduce streaming volume, following Algorithm 2 line 7.
The dead zone [theta, 1.0] (default theta = 0.9) is enforced so that alpha is left unchanged when 0.9 <= rho <= 1, preventing oscillation from bursty PCIe fluctuations.
The threshold theta is exposed as a tunable parameter of the planner with default value 0.9.

Alpha adjustments are gradual (not one-shot swaps of large fractions), so that parameter migration overhead is small and can be overlapped with model forwarding rather than blocking the compute stream.
The memory-aware safety constraint that prioritizes KV cache over expert residency has been implemented.
The planner tracks the total GPU memory budget C_gpu and the current KV cache usage C_kv (measured by generated tokens) and derives the residency budget C_res = C_gpu - C_kv each iteration.
The hard safety constraint C_exp(alpha) <= C_gpu - C_kv is enforced after every alpha update so that expert residency never displaces the KV cache (Algorithm 2 line 9).

Code has been implemented to compute C_exp(alpha), the aggregate on-device size of the fraction alpha of expert parameters (accounting for compressed vs. uncompressed storage), for use in the safety constraint.

When the safety constraint is binding, the planner reduces alpha (even if this pushes tau_load > tau_comp(theory)) to preserve the maximum feasible batch size and concurrency rather than triggering activation swapping.
The runtime, closed-loop control structure of the planner (Algorithm 2) has been implemented.

The planner is structured as an asynchronous control loop that, on each iteration, estimates tau_load, computes rho, adjusts alpha per the threshold policy, and enforces the memory constraint, matching the sequence of steps in Algorithm 2 (lines 1-9).
The planner runs asynchronously with the inference compute stream and does not insert CUDA synchronization primitives on the critical path of model forwarding.

When the planner decides to change alpha, the resulting expert migration (promotion to GPU residency or demotion to host DRAM) reuses the storage-hierarchy transfer path so that parameter movement is overlapped with the next forward pass.

The planner supports the tri-state residency model x + y + z = 1 (uncompressed GPU-resident, compressed GPU-resident, offloaded to host DRAM), and the current prototype instance sets x = 0 so that experts alternate between compressed GPU residency and CPU offloading.
The planner exhibits the stability and convergence behavior described in Section 4.3 and Figure 6.

The planner implements negative feedback control: increasing alpha monotonically decreases estimated tau_load and decreasing alpha monotonically increases it, so that the control loop converges toward a stable operating point.

When GPU memory is sufficient, the planner drives alpha toward the operating point where tau_load approximately equals tau_comp(theory) (the knee of the tau_load vs. alpha curve in Figure 6), rather than staying at alpha = 1.

In behavior consistent with Figure 6, decreasing alpha from 1.0 leaves the measured actual forward latency tau_comp flat while loading remains hidden, and only past the knee does tau_comp increase linearly as the pipeline stalls waiting for expert materialization.
The planner's runtime adaptation produces the measured behavior reported in Exp#3 on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (TP=4, BS=256, context 4096).

In the Exp#3 run on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct, adaptation is first triggered at approximately iteration 2700, when the KV cache footprint approaches the pre-allocated capacity and throughput begins to fluctuate.
After the first adaptation, the planner repeatedly triggers alpha decreases at roughly a 300-iteration cadence, offloading 48 compressed experts per rank (one expert per layer) at each step.
Over the Exp#3 session, alpha is adjusted 7 times in total, offloading 48 * 4 * 7 compressed experts and reclaiming approximately 5.3 GB of GPU memory.

Across the Exp#3 session, the throughput of the dynamic alpha adaptation setting never drops below that of the fixed alpha = 1.0 baseline, confirming that migration overhead is fully hidden within the compute window.
The end-to-end throughput results comparing FluxMoE, vLLM, and vLLM-O on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct under a performance-bound regime (Figure 7) have been reproduced.
The experimental configuration for Exp#1 (performance-bound regime deployment of Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct on 4 GPUs with TP=4) has been set up.
Code has been implemented to deploy Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct with tensor parallelism degree TP=4 across four NVIDIA L40 (48 GB) GPUs on a single node.
Code has been implemented to sweep batch size across the values {32, 64, 128, 256} with the context length fixed at 4,096 tokens for Figure 7(a).
Code has been implemented to sweep context length across the values {1024, 2048, 3072, 4096} tokens with the batch size fixed at 256 for Figure 7(b).
